pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) using place value and properties (7×30 = 7×3 tens = 21 tens = 210).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 use place value and known facts to multiply mentally; underpins Y4 short multiplication and estimation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 — 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (e.g. 9×80, 5×60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.'
• Operational details — the reasoning, not the trick, is the objective: 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21×10 = 210 (associativity + place value). The '×10 shifts digits one place left' understanding must replace the dangerous 'just add a zero' rule (which breaks for decimals later). Use place-value counters/columns and the known fact 7×3=21 scaled by ten. This is the engine of estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and a stepping-stone to × multiples of 100/1000 and to long multiplication.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 3×40 via 3×4 tens with counters. Tier B (age 8–9): any 1-digit × multiple of 10 mentally, explaining via the known fact and place value. Tier C (age 9): explain why the product gains a zero in terms of ten-times-larger, and use the skill to estimate a larger product.
bestPractices: Reason from the known fact scaled by ten: 7×30 = (7×3) tens = 21 tens = 210, using associativity and place value explicitly.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left', NOT 'add a zero', so the idea survives the move to decimals.
Use place-value counters and columns so 21 tens visibly becomes 210 (regrouping ten tens into a hundred).
Connect immediately to estimation — rounding a factor to a multiple of ten to bound a larger product.
Extend the same reasoning to multiples of 100/1000 once secure, keeping the place-value story constant.
keyRepresentations: Place-value counters / columns — 21 tens regrouped to 210
Gattegno/place-value chart — the leftward digit shift for ×10
Number line in tens — skip counting by 30
commonMisconceptions: Over-relying on 'add a zero' as a rule without understanding, which later misfires with decimals (0.7×30).
Multiplying the wrong part (7×30 as 21 rather than 210) — losing the place-value scaling.
Adding an extra or too few zeros through miscounting places.
Not connecting 7×30 to the known fact 7×3, so it's computed from scratch.
Confusing multiplying by a multiple of ten with adding tens.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) by reasoning from a known fact scaled by ten — 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21 tens = 210 — using place value and the associative property. The objective is the reasoning, not the 'add a zero' trick: learners should understand multiplying by 10 as making a number ten times larger so its digits shift one place left, which is why 210 ends in a zero (the ones place empties). This understanding survives the later move to decimals, where 'add a zero' fails (0.7×10 = 7, not 0.70), and powers estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and multiplication by multiples of 100/1000.

activities.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner writes 7×30 = 21, point back to the rods: 'You took three tens seven times, not three ones. Count the tens — 21 tens is 210.'
If a learner gives 210 but only explains 'you add a zero', ask them to show it with the rods: 'Where did that zero come from? Watch the ones column empty when everything grows ten times bigger.'
If a learner miscounts zeros (e.g. 2100), have them regroup the tens carefully onto the place-value chart and reread each column.
Affirm reasoning that names the known fact: 'Yes — knowing 7×3 = 21 let you get 7×30 without starting over.'
activities.rationale: Place-value counters and regrouping make '21 tens = 210' a visible exchange rather than a memorised rule, and tie the standard's required place-value/property strategy directly to the known single-digit fact.
sourceClaims: 3.NBT.3 requires multiplying one-digit numbers by multiples of 10 (10–90) using place-value and property strategies.
Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activities.title: Why 'add a zero' is not the real rule
feedback: If a learner says 0.7×10 = 0.70, show the shift on the chart: 'Sliding left makes 7, not 0.70. The zero rule breaks here — but the shift still works.'
If a learner adds too many or too few zeros for the 7×300 extension, count the place shifts together: '×100 means shifting two columns left.'
Encourage precise language: 'ten times larger' and 'shifts one place left' rather than 'add a zero'.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting the whole-number case with a decimal case targets the misconception that 'add a zero' is the underlying rule, replacing it with the place-value shift that generalises.
sourceClaims: Teach multiplying by ten as a place-value shift (ten times larger) rather than 'adding a zero', which fails for decimals.
learnerActions: On a place-value chart, place 7 in the ones column, then slide it one column left to make 70; describe what happened to the digit.
Do the same with 21: slide it one column left so the ones place becomes empty and a 0 fills it, giving 210.
Now try 0.7×10 on the same chart: slide 0.7 one column left to get 7 — notice no zero was added.
State in your own words why '×10 shifts digits one place left' is safer than 'add a zero'.
(Optional extension, once the tens pattern feels secure) Predict and check 7×300 using the same idea: 7×3 = 21, shifted two places = 2100.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by ten always shifts digits one place to the left; for whole numbers this shows up as a trailing zero, but the shift — not the zero itself — is the real rule, which is why it still works for decimals.

activities.title: Using tens facts to estimate
feedback: If a learner rounds the wrong way or forgets to scale, revisit the known-fact chain: '6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 240.'
If a learner treats the estimate as exact, prompt: 'Is 6×43 more or less than 6×40? By about how much?'
Praise clear connections between the rounded factor and the place-value reasoning.
activities.rationale: Multiplying by multiples of ten is a useful tool for estimation (the standard itself only names place-value and property-based strategies for products in the range 10–90); applying it keeps the place-value story in a purposeful context.
sourceClaims: Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 6×43 by rounding 43 to 40 and computing 6×40 = 240 (6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 24 tens = 240), explaining the reasoning.

(Optional extension, once the tens case is secure) Estimate 234×5 by rounding 234 to 200 and computing 200×5 = 1000 (2×5 = 10, so 200×5 = 10 hundreds = 1000), using the same known-fact-then-scale reasoning.
Compare each estimate to the exact answer (6×43 = 258; 234×5 = 1170) and say whether the estimate is high or low and roughly by how much.
Make up one estimation of your own using a multiple of ten and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of ten (and, by the same reasoning, a multiple of a hundred) lets you quickly bound or approximate a larger product, which checks whether an exact answer is reasonable.

activities.title: Spot and explain the error
feedback: For '7×30 = 21': 'The 30 is three tens, so the answer must be 21 tens = 210 — ten times bigger than 21.'
For '8×40 = 32': 'That's just 8×4. Scale by ten: 32 tens = 320.'
Confirm the correct ones (5×60 = 300 and 9×80 = 720) and ask the learner to articulate the reasoning, not just the verdict.
activities.rationale: Identifying and repairing errors consolidates the reasoning and surfaces whether a learner can justify answers rather than apply a rote appendage; this is a consolidation/check activity that tests fluency rather than a substitute for building the scaling intuition with counters.
learnerActions: Decide whether each worked example is correct: 7×30 = 21; 5×60 = 300; 8×40 = 32; 9×80 = 720.
For any that are wrong, say exactly what went wrong (e.g. multiplied the tens as ones, or dropped/added a zero).
Rewrite each incorrect one with the full reasoning chain to make it correct.
Explain in words why 5×60 = 300 ends in a zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Common slips — multiplying the tens digit as ones, or miscounting zeros — can be caught by checking against the known-fact-times-ten chain.

constraints: The learning objective is the reasoning (known fact × ten via associativity and place value), not a memorised 'add a zero' step; any activity must require the learner to explain where the zero comes from.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left' explicitly, because 'add a zero' misfires for decimals (0.7×10 = 7).
Secure the underlying single-digit fact (e.g. 7×3) first; if it is shaky, the whole derivation is unreliable.

Recognition/multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank checks test fluency but do not by themselves build the scaling intuition; use them for consolidation alongside construction with counters and spoken reasoning.
Physical base-ten equipment and a drawn or on-screen place-value chart are both suitable; manipulatives make the regrouping of ten tens into a hundred concrete.
Extend the identical place-value story to multiples of 100/1000 only once the tens case is secure; the 7×300 step is presented as an optional extension for this reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×3=21 so 7×30=210; 5×6=30 so 5×60=300; 3×4=12 so 3×40=120; 6×4=24 so 6×40=240; 8×4=32 so 8×40=320; 9×8=72 so 9×80=720; 7×3=21 so 7×300=2100; 6×43=258; 234×5=1170; 2×5=10 so 200×5=1000 — all check out. The 'spot the error' items 7×30=21 and 8×40=32 are intentionally incorrect for learners to catch, with corrected values (210, 320) supplied in feedback.
Decimal check: 0.7×10=7 (not 0.70); the shift-left framing is correct and the 'add a zero' rule correctly fails here.
Source note: the CCSS 3.NBT.3 and NCETM claims are marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; retained as cited without upgrading their evidence status.

Original source row legacy vocabulary describing specific interactive formats (e.g. a 'scaler' widget, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) has been generalised into medium-independent learner actions while preserving the live-regrouping mechanism as an optional illustration.

The decimal example (0.7×10), the 200×5 estimation step and the 7×300 extension may exceed the typical age-band comfort zone; all are retained from the original design but flagged as needing teacher judgement/support.

probeDeeper: What does 7 × 30 have to do with 7 × 3?
Why does the answer end in a zero — where does that zero come from?
assess.correctAnswer: 210 and 240. The teacher watches for the child reasoning '7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210' — using the single-digit fact and scaling by ten — rather than a disconnected zero-adding rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies the tens digit as ones — 7×30 treated as 7×3 = 21, forgetting the ten (answer 21)
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 7 × 3 TENS = 21 tens = 210; use base-ten equipment to show three tens taken seven times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer is ten times too small; child computes 7×3 and stops

errorPatterns.pattern: 'adds a zero' as a rote rule with no meaning — works here but cannot say why, and will misapply it to decimals later
errorPatterns.nextMove: tie the zero to 'ten times bigger': multiplying by 30 is multiplying by 3 then by 10, and ×10 shifts digits one place, showing up as a zero for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 210 but explains only 'you add a zero'; cannot connect to 7×3

errorPatterns.pattern: not fluent in the underlying single-digit fact, so the whole derivation is shaky
errorPatterns.nextMove: shore up the single-digit fact before layering the tens reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or errs on 7×3 itself

responseLevels.gap: multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer ten times too small), or has no reasoning at all.
responseLevels.full: reasons via the known fact scaled by ten ('7 × 3 tens = 21 tens'), explains the zero as the result of ×10, and uses the skill to estimate larger products.
responseLevels.partial: gets the right answer via 'add a zero' but cannot connect it to the single-digit fact or explain why the zero appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work out 7 × 30 and 6 × 40 in their head, saying how they did it. Watch whether they use the known fact (7×3) and reason about tens, or whether they just 'add a zero' without understanding — then probe by asking what 7 × 30 has to do with 7 × 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying by a multiple of ten is the first place the 'add a zero' shortcut appears; watching HOW the child reasons (does the zero come from 'ten times', or is it a rote appendage?) reveals whether place-value understanding underpins the shortcut — essential because the same rule misfires later on decimals.
